rv.q: It's a performance of a lifetime, distilling the history of an entire people.
Thank god – whichever one you want – that pretty much every word is riveting.

Its short run at the Ambassadors – a revival of the 2022. Park theatre production, capably directed by Scott Le Crass – is a must-see not only because it is an accomplished play, but because it's an astonishing masterclass in acting by Maureen Lipman.
It’s a terrific feat of concentration, memory and skill.
Funny, shrugging, sad - Lipman was born to play this exhausting feat of a part.
Perched on a wooden bench as the old lady sits shiva for the dead, Lipman makes it all so real, so tangible.
Together, Lipman and Sherman make us marvel – and tremble.
But with Rose never rising from the bench where she sits shiva, it can feel profoundly static.
This is overlong and very static for a solo show and if you lose focus you can miss one of the narrative swerves.
She wows with this still and utterly gripping performance.
Maureen Lipman, whose every gesture, every facial expression and every phrasing of some thoughtful, often witty comment is absolutely riveting.
Minor production gripes aside, this Rose demands to be seen.
Lipman renders Rose's inner dichotomies with understated yet astonishing detail, a Japanese netsuke sculpture humbly glistening on stage.
Maureen Lipman is magical – a master of her craft!
It truly is a masterclass in letting the text shine and Lipman enchants us.

cn.t: Lipman delivers an extraordinary, riveting performance in Sherman's Holocaust survivor monologue, holding audiences spellbound for over two hours. Critics praise her stamina and the play's mix of humor and tragedy, though some find the writing uneven.
